text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's Austrian newspapers.
- Former Finance Minister Hannes Androsch is accusing Chancellor Franz Vranitzky of using political influence, after the supreme administrative court fined him 1.5 million schillings for tax evasion.
- Aluminium maker Austria Metall AG (Amag), one of the last major state-owned firms in Austria, has been sold to its chief executive Klaus Hammerer and industrialist Herbert Turnauer.

- Health Minister Christa Krammer and the representatives of the provinces have agreed on a new hospital reform. Specialist doctors will have to be on call at night. But further steps should be made, she said.
- Employee and employer representatives have agreed on a new ruling for night work. Men and women will now be treated equally, whereas previously women were not allowed to work at night.

- Austria is expected to take part in the first round of the European Monetary Union, say London-based experts at Morgan Grenfell. Even if all the planned privatisations and spending cuts are not completed Austria should be able to take part.
- U.S. paper maker Mead might invest three billion schillings in Austrian paper maker Frantschach's southern Austrian plant in Poels.
- Creditanstalt and Bank Austria are two of three bidders for Hungary's 94 percent stake in Magyar Hitel Bank Rt..
- Opinion polls say, that any one of Austria's top three parties could potentially win nationwide elections.
- Austria's trade deficit in tourism rose by four billion schillings to 29.9 billion in the period from January to August 1996 compared to a year ago.
- Social Democrat union leaders are openly discussing the possibility of Chancellor and party leader Franz Vranitzky being ousted.
- Austria's ATX blue-chip index fell in last minute trade on Wednesday due to heavy selling in shares of industrial group OMV and steel maker VA Stahl.
- Yuji Fujita, Japanese head of metal maker Amada Austria, says Austria is too inflexible and expensive for investments.
- Vienna's state government must cut its deficit to 4.5 billion schillings from eight billion by 1997 to reach Maastricht criteria.
